title: Many-Body Physics with Rydberg Atoms: Quantum Simulation and Non-equilibrium Dynamics
authors: Zhengyang Bai, Cheng Chen, Fan Yang, Weibin Li
abstract: Rydberg atoms, characterized by their strong and long-range dipole-dipole interactions, provide a versatile platform for exploring intriguing collective and many-body effects. Recently, the experimental realization of these effects in dense ensembles and reconfigurable atomic arrays has attracted significant interest, particularly for applications in quantum simulations and non-equilibrium physics. This review focuses on such recent development, discussing the theoretical foundations of the interactions between Rydberg atoms and the ensuing many-body physics, while providing a critical survey of experimental techniques for their precise manipulation and observation. We further discuss recent breakthroughs in leveraging Rydberg collective effects to probe novel many-body phases and non-equilibrium dynamics of these systems. By synthesizing theoretical insights with experimental milestones, we provide a comprehensive perspective on this rapidly evolving field and its transformative potential for future quantum technologies.
summary: This review provides a comprehensive survey of using Rydberg atoms to investigate many-body physics. It covers theoretical tools like the Ising model and LGTs, demonstrating how these are realized experimentally in programmable atomic arrays. The paper highlights breakthroughs in studying non-equilibrium dynamics, topological phases, and quantum simulation potential.
main_problem: The review explores how Rydberg atoms, due to their strong dipole-dipole interactions, can be used as a versatile platform to study complex many-body physics, quantum simulation, and non-equilibrium dynamics.
main_result: Significant progress has been made in observing exotic phases (like topological states) and verifying fundamental dynamic processes (like QKZM) by mapping theoretical models onto programmable Rydberg atom arrays.
method: The paper synthesizes theoretical frameworks (e.g., Ising model, LGTs) with experimental techniques involving adiabatic state preparation, site-resolved measurements, and quench dynamics in atomic ensembles.
model_or_system: The primary system is arrays of Rydberg atoms trapped in optical tweezers or lattices. Key models include the Quantum Ising model ($\hat{H} = \sum \Omega \hat{\sigma}_i^x - \sum V_{ij}\hat{n}_i\hat{n}_j$) and extensions to simulate lattice gauge theories and spin-1/2 XY models.
key_observables: Phase transitions (e.g., crystalline order), correlation growth, entanglement entropy, out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs), and signatures of quantum criticality.
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($V_{ij} \propto 1/R_{ij}^6$), detuning ($\Delta$), blockade radius ($R_b$), and lattice geometry (e.g., Kagome, triangular).
main_assumptions: The review assumes the ability to precisely control atomic interactions and map complex Hamiltonians onto controllable physical platforms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate quantum spin liquid realization on a Kagome lattice via blockade constraints, preparation of random states in 1D arrays, and observation of string-breaking dynamics in a U(1) system.
paper_structure: The review is structured thematically, covering theoretical foundations (interactions), specific physical phenomena (phase transitions, thermalization, LGTs), advanced dynamic studies (QKZM, OTOCs), and applications (optimization).
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it details the cutting edge of using neutral atoms to simulate complex quantum matter models, bridging fundamental condensed matter theory with state-of-the-art experimental quantum optics.
